# How Fields Interact

A payment's amount has more meaning alongside its merchant and the account's
earlier activity. RelFlow builds that context at two scales: fields belonging
to one event record, then events belonging to the same history. This keeps the
relationship between an amount and its merchant available when the model
compares transactions.
Start with [transaction history](../../tutorials/transaction-history.qmd) for
the application example.

This explanation was checked against the [pinned 0.2.4 branch encoder](https://github.com/relflow/relflow/blob/8d9d6cfd8ce22a7819c2b5392c710d4f2cbe1a7c/src/relflow/architecture/encoder.py).

## Within One Transaction

Follow the tutorial's collection. The current payment is the final transaction;
the earlier transactions were known at its decision time:

```yaml
trxns:
  - booked_at: "2026-05-21T10:00:00"
    amount: 32.00
    merchant: Station Cafe
    disputed: false
  - booked_at: "2026-05-27T18:15:00"
    amount: 56.20
    merchant: North Market
    disputed: true
  - booked_at: "2026-05-28T14:30:00"
    amount: 84.50
    merchant: North Market
    disputed: false
```

Each field first supplies an embedding at each transaction coordinate.
Coordinate attention groups the direct sibling fields at the same coordinate:
`booked_at`, `amount`, and `merchant` from the first transaction interact with one
another. The other transactions have their own groups. This step allows an amount's
representation to depend on the merchant attached to that amount.

`disputed=rf.Boolean(mask=True)` keeps every dispute label out of the inputs
and supervises every retained transaction. Each label means a new dispute
during the 30 days after the common review cutoff,
`2026-05-28T14:30:00`. The application attaches these Boolean answers after
that window is complete; they are not facts available to the model at review.

Two histories can have the same total spend and merchant counts while pairing
the larger purchase with different merchants. Keeping each transaction's
fields together preserves that distinction as evidence for learning.

The coordinate encoder operates on active direct leaf fields. A nested branch
contributes its own representation later; it does not join this group of direct
fields. When fewer than two active direct fields are available, there is no
coordinate interaction to perform. Setting branch attention to `None` also
disables this encoder.

## Across The History

After coordinate attention, the branch concatenates its children's tokens into
one sequence and applies its sequence encoder. Tokens from different history
positions can now interact. Across a longer history, the model can learn
patterns such as repeated purchases at one merchant, changing amounts, or
activity concentrated in a short period. Whether these patterns help predict
a dispute must be checked on held-out payments.

These two stages answer different questions:

| Stage | Available context | Example relationship |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Coordinate attention | Direct fields of one transaction | Which merchant received this amount? |
| Sequence attention | Present child tokens across the branch | How does this transaction compare with earlier ones? |
| Branch reduction | The branch's encoded transactions | Which context should reach the observation root? |

Reduction is a separate step, described in [Branch Summaries](branch-reduction.qmd).
With the default reduction, `trxns` passes a learned summary to its parent.
That summary includes the earlier and latest transactions; the root has no
duplicate amount or merchant fields. The summary is trained for the model's
objectives; it is not a readable transaction ledger or a guaranteed calculation
of a business statistic.

## Presence And Position

Padding represents an absent coordinate. The encoder excludes it from attention
and restores zero output at absent positions. A null value at a present
coordinate has its own field state; replacing it with zero changes what the
model observes. See [field states](../../core-concepts/data-types.qmd).

Rotary position information gives attention a signal about token positions.
`booked_at=rf.DateParts(dateparts=["day_of_month", "day_of_week", "hour_of_day"])`
supplies calendar cycles. Those cycles do not compute elapsed time or preserve
every distinction in the original timestamp. Input ordering still belongs to
the application: sort by the full booking timestamp, oldest to newest, and
keep only transactions available through the latest payment's decision time.
Position information does not repair an incorrectly ordered collection or
prevent future information from entering the inputs.

Sequence attention can use the complete retained collection. All predictions
in this example share the same review cutoff and future outcome window. They
are not forecasts made separately at each transaction's original booking time.

Encoder updates use residual attention and feed-forward blocks with RMSNorm and
tanh GELU, as defined in the [pinned neural blocks](https://github.com/relflow/relflow/blob/8d9d6cfd8ce22a7819c2b5392c710d4f2cbe1a7c/src/relflow/architecture/blocks.py).
Architecture options and collection limits belong in the
[model tree](../../core-concepts/model-tree.qmd) and [Branch reference](../../data-types/branch.qmd).
